entry.title: A timeout is not a failed action: chaos-testing agent tool calls
entry.summary: Arjun Garg (Intuit) at Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2026 on injecting a lost reply after an agent's tool call commits, and how retries stay safe.
entry.content:
An agent places an order, the service creates it, and the reply never arrives. The agent sees a timeout, retries, and now there are two orders. At Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2026, Arjun Garg of Intuit shows how to make that failure observable with a small public MCP reproduction, then turns it into a chaos test plan for any agent tool that mutates something.

He is explicit that the experiment uses synthetic effects, that it is not evidence of an incident at an employer or a vendor, and that he speaks in a personal capacity. What he offers is a familiar distributed-systems boundary, replayed with an MCP client and server.

Why can't a better prompt fix a lost reply?

The service knows it appended a record. The caller knows a response didn't arrive before its deadline. "Neither observation cancels the other," Arjun says, and a handler that turns every timeout into a new business operation is making a consequential policy choice with incomplete evidence.

That is why longer timeouts, better prompts or telling the model to be careful don't close the gap. They may change how often it happens. They don't establish what happened during one particular ambiguous attempt. The question he wants you to keep in mind is what new evidence would make the next mutation justified.

What does the reproduction show?

The setup uses a real SDK client and server over in-memory streams. A relay watches the first tool response and drops it after the handler has returned, so the effect is already recorded when the reply disappears. The client's read timeout then raises an MCP error, and the script does exactly one application-level retry. The SDK doesn't retry on its own. No sleeps coordinate the fault.

Two runs are compared. The baseline ends with two effects. The positive control carries a logical operation ID and returns the earlier effect identifier on the repeat. The fault stays identical and only duplicate suppression changes, so the property being tested is isolated. Arjun is careful about the limits: it is an in-memory, sequential illustration, and it does not show durability across restarts, concurrent exclusion or safe integration with a separate downstream service.

Four identifiers, four different meanings

A big part of the talk is vocabulary. An RPC identifier correlates messages. An attempt identifier explains a dispatch. A logical operation identifier says "this is the same intent". An effect reference points at what actually happened. They can all sit in one trace and still mean different things.

This is why hashing the whole argument object misleads, since attempt metadata changes between tries. Even a hash of only the business arguments can't tell retrying one order from deliberately buying the same items twice. The caller or a trusted workflow has to make that call, and the receiver needs a scope and a contract for honouring it.

Where reserving a key goes wrong

If a gateway reserves a key, calls an external service, then stores the receipt, a crash after the external commit but before the receipt write leaves an intent record with no completion evidence. Reserve first and you can stop a second worker but leave the operation unresolved. Write only afterwards and a crash leaves no local record even though the effect happened. A local transaction can't atomically include an arbitrary remote API, so recovery needs the provider's cooperation: idempotency, lookup by operation reference, or a documented reconciliation procedure.

The fault-injection matrix changes the fault location in each row, and so changes what you know afterwards: before dispatch, after reservation, after remote commit, after receipt persistence, after retention expiry. A test harness should record which barrier it reached before injecting the fault, and the assertion isn't always a successful retry. Sometimes the right result is a bounded unresolved state with an owner and a reconciliation route.

Arjun also lists four assertion types that aren't interchangeable: effect count (catches duplicates), result integrity, progress (is anyone able to resolve unfinished work), and freshness (a stale worker waking up after a takeover). Refunds make the point: a system can block the second refund and still leave support unable to tell whether the first one happened.

The recovery decision tree

His rule of thumb for a mutating agent tool: look for evidence of completion first, and return the original result if you can. If you have reliable proof of non-execution and stale workers are fenced out, a new dispatch may be appropriate. If the provider supports idempotent retry with the same key, use that contract even when the first outcome is ambiguous. Otherwise preserve the ambiguity and reconcile. A human clicking approve doesn't prove the first effect never happened.

Cancellation and backoff don't help here. MCP cancellation lets the recipient ignore the notification if work already completed, so it isn't a rollback, and waiting longer doesn't tell you whether the first order exists. Keep an oracle independent of the system under test, include the deliberately unprotected baseline to prove the oracle can see duplicates, and log the operation key, effect evidence and final caller status together.

The line he closes on: "The timeout tells us that the caller lacks a response. It does not tell us that the service lacks an order."

Who should watch

Anyone giving an agent tools that charge, refund, create, send or delete. It is a careful, qualified talk with slides about boundaries rather than a product demo, and it will be most useful to people who already own retry logic. If you only need the one-sentence takeaway, it is above; the matrix and the decision tree are the reason to watch.

Related Conf42 talks: Surviving a 300% Flash Crowd: State-Safe Autoscaling With Zero Split-Brain Events by Amit Singh Negi of T-Mobile, Your Backup Is Not Your Recovery by Praveen Kumar Gopalakrishnan of Salesforce, and Your Agent Failed Mid-Run. Logs Won't Replay It. by Reza Amini of Flashback at MLOps 2026.

entry.title: SREday Chennai is free, two tracks, at Hexaware HQ on December 5
entry.summary: SREday Chennai runs December 5, 2026 at Hexaware HQ in Siruseri - a free, two-track day on SRE, DevOps and cloud. Apply on Luma to get a seat.
entry.content:
SREday Chennai happens on December 5, 2026, at Hexaware HQ in Siruseri, Chennai: a one-day, two-track conference on site reliability engineering, DevOps and cloud. It is free to attend, and seats go to people who apply on Luma and are approved.

If you know SREday from London, Amsterdam or the other cities, the format is the same: practitioners on stage, breaks built into the schedule, and a lobby where the real arguments about alert fatigue happen.

What the day looks like

The plan on the event page is a single day with two rooms running in parallel, a coffee break before the talks, lunch and networking after the first block, and a networking and sponsor crawl later in the afternoon. The day starts at 09:30 India time. The event page lists 20+ speakers across the two tracks.

Hexaware hosts the day, with Harness among the sponsors.

The lineup

The speaker list is still being put together, and the schedule appears on the SREday Chennai page once it is published. We will not guess at names here. What we can say is what SREday programmes tend to cover, because the brand has a clear scope: incident response and postmortems, observability, Kubernetes and platform engineering, cloud cost, and, increasingly, what happens when AI agents start touching production systems.

If you would rather be on stage than in the audience, the call for papers sits at cfp.ninja. The talks that land best at SREday are real stories: the outage, the migration, the runbook that lied.

Why a Conf42 viewer should go

Conf42 runs online, which is great for watching a talk at 2x speed and terrible for asking the speaker a follow-up question. SREday is the in-person half. If Conf42 Site Reliability Engineering 2026 or Conf42 DevSecOps 2026 is in your watch history, Chennai is the room where those conversations continue, with a lunch break to keep arguing through.

It is also a rare free conference at a company campus, which makes it an easy sell to your manager: no ticket, no expense report, one day.

How to get in

Registration is free on Luma. Fill in the application and wait for the approval; since seats are approved one by one, apply sooner rather than later. Updates on speakers and the schedule land on the event page first.

entry.title: LLMday Montevideo bets that the harness matters more than the model
entry.summary: LLMday Montevideo, December 5 at World Trade Center Montevideo - Zyte, IBM, Abstracta, Marvik and Blizzard on agents, RAG and AI security. CONF42 = 42% off.
entry.content:
LLMday Montevideo is on December 5, 2026, at the World Trade Center Montevideo, and a good part of the programme argues one thing: what makes an agent work in production is everything around the model. Speakers come from Zyte, IBM, Abstracta, Marvik, Nubiral, Loopstudio, TCS and Blizzard Entertainment, and the code CONF42 takes 42% off the ticket.

The day has two rooms: the Main Stage all day, and the Ephemeral Stage opening after lunch.

Three talks with "harness" in the title

That is not a coincidence. Joaquin Bonifacino (Zyte) gives Long Running Agents: The Harness Is the Product, drawn from an agentic data-QA engine running at 20B+ tokens per week. His point: demos run for thirty seconds, production agents run for hours, and most of what breaks at that timescale has nothing to do with the model.

Martin Brian (Marvik) turns the same question into a game in The Harness Auction: What Makes an AI Agent Actually Work?. Every audience member gets a limited budget and bids on components: a better model, tools, skills, more context, subagents or a verification loop. Bring a strategy.

Lucia Hernandez (Metodica Digital) widens the definition in The User Is Part of the Harness: A Year Running an Agent That Adapts to Cognitive Load, built around her own inconsistent executive function after an autism diagnosis at 35.

RAG, documents and the boring wins

Josefina R. Casanova (IBM) shares From PDFs to Production RAG: Lessons from Building Document Pipelines with Docling, and Leon Achata (TCS) argues RAG Is Not a Search Problem, since exact identifiers, jargon and paraphrases all need different retrieval. Marcos Martinez (Loopstudio) has the most concrete number on the bill: From 1 Hour to 10 Minutes: Automating Purchase Orders with AI, for a US food and beverage distributor that received about 100 purchase orders a day by email, each in its own layout.

Roger Abelenda (Abstracta) presents Tero, an open-source agent platform for quality intelligence, and Gorka Ludlow (Karma Digital) ships Apps, not chats: macOS products that run models on-device.

Security and the bigger picture

Martin Rojas breaks the GenAI data pipeline with OWASP guidance, and Federico Novelli (Protect Group) asks how to turn prompt injection and excessive agent permissions into business risk a security team can act on. Axel Labruna and Maika de Jesus Esteves (Nubiral) cover AgentOps, Fede Rodrigo insists AI Is Never the Starting Point, and Marcelo B San Martin (Blizzard Entertainment) closes the Ephemeral Stage with The Great AI Role Rewrite.

For a change of pace, Mark Pawlikowski and Marcos Novelli Harispe (Reliaburger) run a workshop that is openly a non-LLM break: set up, test and break a production cluster in seconds.

Why a Conf42 viewer should go

If you followed the agent and RAG talks at Conf42 Large Language Models 2026, Montevideo is where you can bid against the people who gave them. The local community shows up too, with OWU, AWS Girls User Group Uruguay and DOUG Brazil on the supporters list.

Register

Registration opens at 08:00. Tickets are on Luma with CONF42 for 42% off, and the two-stage schedule is on the LLMday Montevideo page.

entry.title: Conf42 MLOps 2026: a green check is not a fact
entry.summary: The Conf42 MLOps 2026 roundup - 53 talks on agents that fail quietly, evals that check what happened, identity for agents and governance in the pipeline.
entry.content:
Conf42 MLOps 2026 premiered on November 19 with 53 talks, and the event's own tagline did most of the framing: training the model is the easy part. The hard part, according to speakers from Microsoft AI, Okta, JPMorgan Chase, Amazon, Walmart Global Tech, OpenAI, Aflac and a long list of smaller teams, is knowing whether the thing you shipped did what it says it did. Again and again the talks came back to the same uncomfortable observation. The request succeeded, the JSON parsed, the dashboard stayed green, and the result was still wrong.

Most of the program was about agents, but the classic MLOps work was well represented too: training data, labels, edge inference, GPUs and pipelines that auditors can replay.

Agents fail quietly, so the checks have to look elsewhere

Muhammad Haris Farooq of Ruby AI runs more than 50 types of agents and about 3,800 production runs a month, and he opened with a bug where nothing was broken: prompt caching was switched on, yet the cache hit rate sat at 0% for months because the code flattened the system prompt into one string and dropped the cache markers. "They don't fail loudly, they fail quietly, and they still give you something that looks fine," Muhammad Haris Farooq said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. His fixes are plain engineering: math, formatting and data changes go to code, every run is priced, and drawing the dependency graph of 13 sequential agents took a research job from a median of 32.5 minutes to about 10.7.

Danila Redikultsev of Aeroclub gave the theme its name. In his rebuilt support store, a refund passes every policy check and still goes to the wrong order, because the one value the check never questioned, the order ID, was picked by the model. He calls that self-signed evidence, and a second model did not save him: asked to review 72 wrong refunds, an LLM judge approved every one. "A green check is not a fact. It's a question. Who signed it?" Danila Redikultsev said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

Several talks cover the same ground from the guardrail side. Dylan Merigaud of Merigaud Consulting compares rules written as sentences with rules enforced in code on the path of the action, from a preregistered replay of 5 rules and 200 runs. Michael Oskola of Retailbox shares the build log of an agent fleet where every fact passes a write-gate before it can be remembered, and Shipra Sonal and Madhu Gurramkonda of Amazon describe a validator that checks every claim in a draft answer against its live source.

Evals that check what actually happened

Sajal Garg of Microsoft AI split an agent run into three records that can disagree: what the reply claims, which tool the agent tried to use, and what the service says changed. His worked example, a training job that must be submitted once and only after approval, turns into a repeatable test where the reply is an input to the check and never its own answer key.

Reza Amini of Flashback attacked the step before the eval: reproducing the failure. His warehouse agent reserves three pallets when the customer ordered three cartons, and rerunning it live would hit the real systems again and might take a different path. His answer is record, replay, fork: save every model and tool call to a file, replay it offline, then fork from the first wrong call and run live only from there.

The abstract-only half of the evals track points the same way. Dylan Ler of Adobe argues for evals as a deployment artifact, Raju Dandigam of Navan turns an agent trace into a regression test that runs in CI, Anwar Khan of John Deere covers eval-as-code, and Ocean Coldiron of ModMed tests an LLM that writes clinical configuration, where a wrong answer becomes a patient-safety ticket.

Who is calling, and on whose behalf?

The security talks were mostly about identity. Bhavik Thakkar of Okta started from the shared API key that most ML platforms still run on. "If you have the key, you are in, and nobody can tell one caller from another," Bhavik Thakkar said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. His bar for every model call is three questions: who is calling, on whose behalf, and allowed to do what, answered through five building blocks with a SPIFFE example.

Ajay Munjuluru of JPMorgan Chase pointed out that agent eval suites score accuracy, helpfulness and cost, and none of those checks care who is asking. He tests for permission leaks with personas, takes the expected results from the source system instead of from the test author, and lets a failure block the release. Nishanth Vepachedu made the sharpest version of the argument for incident agents: diagnosis is the easy bit and authority is the hard part, because such an agent holds production privileges while reading logs that anyone who can send a request helped write.

Kriti Faujdar of Yelp mapped the attack surface as four layers, from the model through agents and tools down to infrastructure, and Jose Manuel Ortega of Alicante University covered security strategies for the MLOps pipeline itself.

Governance becomes a pipeline stage

Shanker Valipireddy of Aflac brought the regulated-enterprise view in three lessons: give every agent an identity, gate actions by risk instead of by hope, and treat evaluation as a release gate that has to keep passing. Arpita Sheth started with an auditor's email asking what data trained the production model, who approved it and how it has behaved since launch, then built the answer in five layers on top of the registry, CI/CD and monitoring a team already has. Ankur Mehra applied the same discipline to valuing loans that have no market price: every ingestion batch gets a timestamp and a hash, and rejected data goes to a dead letter queue instead of into a number someone signs off on.

From the abstracts, Ankur Gupta of Roblox and OWASP presents a rules engine for AI use case governance with policy defined in YAML, Joao Marques of Asqav covers hash-chained, signed audit trails for agents, and Neelima Verma measures fairness in dollars on 95,588 real mortgage applications.

From a demo to a page with real traffic

Artem Zamarajev of Amazon talked about LLM features that live on a web page, with a made-up coffee store as the running example. His first two lessons are to precompute by default and to keep the model off the critical path, with a fallback ladder decided before anyone writes a prompt: fresh content, then the last good version, then a plain non-AI default. Meher Bhaskar Madiraju of Walmart Global Tech set model capability against outcomes and went through the failure modes between a proof of concept and production one by one.

The inference track goes below the API. Alessandro Vozza of Volt Datacenters follows a single token from an agent in Kubernetes to vLLM on bare-metal GPUs and back, Kosseila Haddalene of Cloudthrill shares a Terraform-driven vLLM stack for EKS, AKS, GKE and Nebius, and Nishant Modak of Last9 joins GPU telemetry to the Kubernetes workload that owns it. Phoebe Wang of OpenAI showed a narrow, read-only Flyte MCP tool that lets Codex look up a failed training run from its link and say which step broke.

Data, labels and small models still decide the result

The least fashionable result of the event came from Vladimir Beskorovainyi of Besk Tech: on noisy product names from receipts, a character n-gram logistic regression beat a 1D CNN and an LSTM in 30 cells out of 30 on his public synthetic benchmark. It was also the slowest of the cheap models, which is where his talk gets interesting.

Devavrat Khanolkar of Cisco Systems explained exposure bias in ranking systems, where items a user never saw get logged as impressions and end up as false negatives in the training data. Nicolo Brandizzi of Fraunhofer IAIS gave a beginner's tour of how web-scale text becomes LLM training data, and Deborah Adedigba of the UK Ministry of Defence asked what you need to see before anyone relies on a skin lesion classifier that scores well in a notebook. At the edge, RanjithKumar Ragavan of T-Mobile traced a six-kilobyte network from PyTorch training to on-device Android inference with ExecuTorch in his personal open source project, and Layth Ayache of Achour Holding covers the MLOps under a Lebanese Sign Language dataset of more than 40,000 samples that had to be built from nothing.

Thanks to the sponsors

Harness and LLMday were the diamond sponsors, with the Prompt Engineering Conference as gold sponsor and HockeyStick as podcast partner, alongside media partners including Manning Publications and Packt.

Every talk is on the Conf42 MLOps 2026 page and in the YouTube playlist. Next in the series is Conf42 Chaos Engineering 2026 on December 3, a fitting follow-up for anyone who now wants to break their own checks on purpose, and Conf42 DevOps 2027 opens the new year on January 21.

entry.title: Agents need a map of your delivery system, not a longer tool list
entry.summary: Sunil Gattupalle (Harness) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on giving agents a typed knowledge graph of software delivery instead of raw API payloads and tool lists.
entry.content:
Give an agent your REST API spec and it knows what each endpoint does. It has no idea when to call it. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Sunil Gattupalle, Engineering Architect at Harness, argued that this missing "when" is the context agents lack in software delivery, and showed how Harness models it as a knowledge graph of entities, events, metrics and relationships that agents query in one language.

It's a vendor talk about a vendor system, and Sunil says so by working in Harness's own terms throughout. But the modelling ideas travel well beyond Harness, and the half of the talk on why raw tool lists make agents worse is useful to anyone building MCP servers.

Why does the API spec leave agents guessing?

Sunil starts with a short history of enterprise software: systems of record, then systems of engagement, then automation with CI/CD and Kubernetes. Reasoning is the next layer, where a system picks dynamic actions at run time instead of replaying behaviour someone coded in advance.

The catch sits in the contract. "The part that is not present in the API specification is when do you use it," Sunil said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. That reasoning used to live in documentation or in the developer's head. For agents it has to be codified and handed over as context.

Delivery makes it sharper. Generating code has become easy, and the rest of the pipeline has to absorb that pace of change while keeping its guardrails, which he calls non-negotiable in enterprise software. Coding can afford flexibility; the further right you move towards production, the more determinism you want, without switching off the agent's ability to reason.

What goes into the graph?

Across every Harness module, the team sorted data into four buckets:

  • Entities: the things you touch, such as pipelines, services, environments, artifacts, vulnerabilities and teams, each with a lifecycle.
  • Events: immutable, point-in-time facts that happen to entities.
  • Metrics: aggregations over events or lifecycles.
  • Relationships: the edges, which Sunil describes as the part that makes the graph traversable.

The path he keeps returning to runs from pull request to commit to artifact, to artifact registry, to a pipeline, to an environment and finally to a running service. Because Harness runs those pipelines, it can see the whole path.

The incident question shows why that matters. Sunil's team asks the same thing every time: what changed? "Something must have changed, whether it is configuration that changed, whether it is code that has changed," he said. Answering it is a traversal: which service, how and when it was deployed, which artifact, which commit, which policy applied to the pipeline, which team owns it. The graph encodes that mental model as metadata so an agent can pick the relevant subgraph instead of rediscovering it.

How does an agent query it?

Each entity type is declared with its dimensions, the operations allowed on them and a note on when to use the type. The graph is hydrated as you use the product: triggering a pipeline, scanning, creating commits and integrating Jira, GitHub and PagerDuty all land in a data lake, normalised and partitioned by tenant. Every query is scoped by the caller's RBAC permissions.

On top sits a SQL-like query language the talk calls HQL. The agent's loop is:

  1. Discover which types exist in the account.
  2. Pick the ones relevant to the question.
  3. Drill into their dimensions, which is the equivalent of choosing projections, predicates and aggregations.
  4. Validate the query it built.
  5. Execute and return results.

The design point is the vocabulary. Sunil's team could have exposed all this through MCP as long tool lists with raw API payloads, and says that would have polluted the context window and made the agent reason worse. Typed, declared metadata gives the agent grounded data to work from, and "they just need to learn one language".

What did the demo show?

On Harness's own environment, which Sunil calls "Harness on Harness", he asks the agent to explain the path from commit to artifact to deployment to environment. The thought process on screen goes breadth first (list the metadata), then narrows to a subgraph and goes depth first, validating each query before executing it. He then asks the AI to visualise the answer, which produces a dashboard whose query you can inspect in code mode, and shows a worker agent for pipeline failure analysis that takes a look-back window and an org and project filter and returns a report on the past thirty days of executions. Inference can go through your own LLM gateway via a connector.

Sunil also mentions that some models seem to prefer the Harness CLI over MCP for the same graph, and that delivery and runtime context in a coding agent adds blast radius and ownership to what the code alone can tell it.

Who should watch

Platform and MLOps engineers wondering what context their agents are missing, and anyone designing an MCP server who suspects that more tools is not the answer. If you want a vendor-neutral benchmark of knowledge graphs against plain tool calling, this isn't it: there are no numbers comparing the two, and the product sections assume you use Harness.

Related Conf42 talks: Agent Evals That Check What Actually Happened by Sajal Garg of Microsoft AI at the same event, Your Agent Failed Mid-Run. Logs Won't Replay It. by Reza Amini of Flashback, and Jimmy Caputo's Agentic Engineering Platforms from Harness at Platform Engineering 2026.

Watch Sunil Gattupalle's talk from Conf42 MLOps 2026.

From Harness

Sunil says the knowledge graph is available to Harness customers through Harness AI chat, the hosted or self-hosted Harness MCP server, the Harness CLI and custom dashboards. The graph is built as you use Harness; you don't have to ask for it.

  • Harness: harness.io
  • Free plan sign-up: app.harness.io

entry.title: SecMLOps: treat every model file as untrusted code
entry.summary: Jose Manuel Ortega (Alicante University) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on securing the ML lifecycle: pickle files, poisoned data, registries and endpoints.
entry.content:
Loading a pre-trained model can run someone else's code with your credentials before a single prediction is made. That is the example Jose Manuel Ortega, security researcher and lecturer at Alicante University, uses at Conf42 MLOps 2026 to show why the DevSecOps practice you already have stops short of the machine learning lifecycle. His talk is a stage-by-stage tour of what he calls SecMLOps, with an open source tool named for almost every gap.

Your scanners do not look where the models live

Jose's starting point is a comparison. Existing DevSecOps handles source code, containers, infrastructure as code and signed, versioned artifacts well. Machine learning adds things that practice was not built for: data that shapes behaviour, models that are non-deterministic and so resist a simple pass/fail security unit test, artifacts that are opaque binaries, and attack types such as evasion, extraction, model inversion and membership inference that have no classical equivalent.

Meanwhile feature stores, experiment trackers, model registries and inference endpoints are rarely in scope for vulnerability scanners. He maps each lifecycle stage to its attack: poisoning at the data stage, malicious dependencies and compromised notebooks at training, tampering and unsigned models at the registry, adversarial samples and extraction at serving, and undetected drift at monitoring, which is how a successful attack stays invisible. For a shared vocabulary between security and data science he points to the OWASP Machine Learning Security Top 10, MITRE ATLAS and the NIST AI Risk Management Framework.

A model file is a program

Most model formats historically rely on Python pickle, and here the talk gets concrete. "A pickle is not a data format," Jose Manuel Ortega said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. Loading one executes whatever the file tells Python to execute, so a user who thinks they are loading weights can end up running an attacker's command with their own data access.

His mitigation is to treat every model file as untrusted code and scan it before loading. The tool he shows is ModelScan, an open source scanner that reads the file byte by byte looking for unsafe code signatures and ranks findings as critical, high, medium or low. It covers formats used by PyTorch, TensorFlow, Keras and scikit-learn, and it runs about as fast as your machine can read the file.

Poisoning happens before the model exists

Data poisoning is nearly invisible afterwards. Jose lists three forms: label flipping, backdoor or trigger attacks that look perfect in evaluation and misbehave on demand, and abuse of a feed the attacker can influence. His principle is that "the data pipeline is a security boundary" and so it needs validation gates, where most teams have a transformation script.

The code example defines a strict Pydantic model for each record, with an amount constrained to a range and a label that must be zero or one. Rows that fail go to quarantine for audit. Then the batch's label distribution is compared with history: a sudden jump in fraud labels is a fingerprint of label flipping and gets flagged before training. Great Expectations does the same job for schemas, value ranges and statistical distributions.

For dependencies the recipe is to freeze, scan and sign: pip-tools for hashed lock files, a software bill of materials you can query the next time a big CVE drops, pip-audit and Safety for known vulnerabilities, and Sigstore's cosign to verify that an artifact was signed by your key before deployment.

The registry is a production artifact repository

Whether it is MLflow or SageMaker Model Registry, the registry deserves production controls. Jose names three attacks: an unauthorized model swap by someone with too much access, weight tampering that changes behaviour without any code diff, and a stage gate bypass where an unapproved model skips evaluation. The defences are role-based access control on who can register and promote, plus hashing the artifact on write and verifying it on load.

At the endpoint, the hardening example has four parts: authentication on every call so access can be scoped and revoked, Pydantic input validation that rejects extra fields and malformed vectors, per-identity rate limiting with SlowAPI because extraction and adversarial probing need volume, and minimal outputs. Return a class label and keep the full probability vector to yourself, since every extra digit of confidence helps someone attempting model inversion. To test your own models first, he recommends the Adversarial Robustness Toolbox.

Security as a stage that cannot be skipped

The last section wires it into CI/CD: signed commits and protected branches, an SBOM at build, policy as code with Open Policy Agent or Checkov at the gate, signature checks at admission and canary rollouts. On identity he asks for separate roles across dev, staging and production, short-lived credentials, secrets in HashiCorp Vault or a cloud secrets manager, and Gitleaks and TruffleHog scanning repositories and notebooks.

Monitoring gets a security reading too. A quality drop or input shift, watched with a tool like Evidently, can be poisoning or an adversarial campaign. And incident runbooks need ML-specific entries, because, in his words, a generic security playbook "won't tell the on-call engineer to roll back a model version".

Who should watch

ML platform engineers and security engineers who have been handed the model pipeline and need a checklist with tool names attached. It is a survey at intermediate level: broad coverage, short code samples, no single topic explored at length. The recording is delivered at a slow, careful pace, and the slides carry the structure well. Specialists in adversarial ML will know the attack taxonomy already.

  • Securing the AI Stack: From Models to Agents to Infrastructure by Kriti Faujdar at Conf42 MLOps 2026.
  • Your SBOM Stops at the model by Emmy Eide at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.
  • When AI Joins the Request Path: Securing API-Backed AI Systems by Jayakumar Ramalingam at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.

entry.title: Prompts are not a permission system: identity for agents and pipelines
entry.summary: Bhavik Thakkar (Okta) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on replacing shared API keys with workload identity, delegation and short-lived scoped tokens for agents.
entry.content:
Ask most ML platform teams who is calling their model and the honest answer is that somebody holding the shared API key is. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Bhavik Thakkar, Senior Product Manager at Okta working on identity and authorization for AI agents, argues that every model call should answer three questions: who is calling, on whose behalf, and allowed to do what. He then walks through five building blocks that get you there using open standards, with no vendor required.

The shared key was a fair trade until agents showed up

Bhavik sorts the callers into three groups: pipelines and ML jobs (nightly training, CI pushing a model to the registry, hourly batch scoring), services (inference endpoints calling the feature store), and AI agents. An agent decides at runtime which tools and models to call, often acts for a specific person, and can be manipulated by what it reads.

Almost none of these callers type a password, and most authenticate with one long-lived key. He lists what happens as the caller count grows. The key gets copied into notebooks, CI variables, laptop environment files and now MCP server config files. It carries the union of everyone's permissions. The logs show that the key was used and nothing about which job used it. And rotating it breaks every caller at once, so nobody rotates it and it lives for years.

Identity should come from where the code runs

Building block one is workload identity: the platform attests the workload (namespace, service account, container image, repository and branch) and hands it a short-lived identity document. Bhavik covers two routes. SPIFFE gives each workload a URI-style ID and a verifiable credential, issued and rotated by SPIRE, typically every hour or less. OIDC workload federation does the same job with tokens that most clouds and CI systems already issue.

His worked example is a retailer running hundreds of agents. The admin sets up trust between the auth server and the company's SPIFFE trust domain once. After that, an inventory agent presents its SPIFFE credential in place of a client secret and gets back a scoped, short-lived OAuth access token. The API it calls only ever sees a standard token. In his words, "you add the hundred and first agent without creating a hundred and first secret".

Block two is delegation. A support rep asks an assistant to summarise a customer's last five tickets. If the agent uses its own broad credentials it can read every ticket in the company. With OAuth token exchange (RFC 8693) the agent presents the user's token plus its own identity and receives a token that names both: the user as subject, the agent as actor. Block three swaps the forever-key for tokens that live for minutes and cover one task. His tip is to start coarse, with one scope per model and one per tool, and to keep scope decisions in the auth server's policy so you can change them without redeploying agents.

The model decides what it wants, the auth layer decides what it gets

The section most agent builders should replay is about MCP. A system prompt that says "only read records, never delete anything" is a hope. "Prompts are not a permission system," Bhavik Thakkar said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. A support ticket with hidden text asking to export every customer's email will get past a check that lives in the model's judgment.

The fix is to authorize at the tool. Under the MCP authorization spec an MCP server acts as an OAuth resource server and, on every tool call, validates the token, checks it was issued for this server, and checks the scope for that tool and that user. A tricked model can ask for the export; the export tool refuses because the token does not carry the scope.

He also covers how a server knows which agent client is connecting. Hand registration does not scale and open Dynamic Client Registration leaves thousands of anonymous one-off records. Client ID Metadata Documents make the client ID an HTTPS URL that the server fetches, which anchors the client to a domain somebody controls.

Approvals people don't learn to ignore, and a kill switch you have timed

Block four is human approval for irreversible or sensitive actions: deleting data, sending external email, deploying to production, moving money. Synchronous confirmation works when the user is in the session; for background agents he points to OpenID's CIBA, where an approver gets a push on a trusted device and the agent waits for its token. Ask for everything and approval turns into theater, so ask only for what matters and let approvals expire with the task.

Block five is audit and revocation. Log six things per call: the caller, the user, the grant and scope, the model and version, the data touched, and the approval. Then practise revocation like a disaster recovery drill: pick one agent in staging and time how long it takes to cut it off. With short-lived tokens that is minutes, and every other caller keeps running.

He closes with four failure patterns (over-scoped tokens, the confused deputy, invisible agent-to-agent hops, the missing kill switch) and six steps to start with.

Who should watch

ML platform engineers, security engineers and anyone putting an MCP server in front of real data. It is a vendor-neutral reference-architecture talk with diagrams and no live demo. If you already run SPIRE and token exchange in production, the MCP and CIMD sections are the new material.

entry.title: A four-floor security map for the AI stack, and the floor teams skip
entry.summary: Kriti Faujdar (Yelp) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on a four-layer defense-in-depth map for AI systems: model, agents, tools and MCP, infrastructure.
entry.content:
An AI demo takes an afternoon, and the launch stalls for months on everything the demo skipped. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Kriti Faujdar, Lead Product Manager at Yelp, where she works on agentic systems after leading security foundation model work at Microsoft Security, hands teams a map of where production AI gets attacked: four layers (model, agents, tools and MCP, infrastructure), the threats on each, and the fixes. Her pick for the layer most teams overlook is the third one.

Her picture is a building. Each floor has its own doors to lock, and a great lock on the front door does nothing about the ground floor window. "an attacker only needs one layer to fail", Kriti Faujdar said at Conf42 MLOps 2026, so the job is to make every floor annoying to get through.

The model cannot tell instructions from data

Layer one is the model itself: direct prompt injection, indirect prompt injection, jailbreaks and output hijacking. Direct injection is the user typing an override into the input. Indirect injection is the one she says people worry about most, because the user does nothing wrong. The attack sits in an email, a shared document, a web page or a calendar invite, the app pulls it into the prompt as relevant context, and input validation never sees it. Her real-world case is published research in which instructions hidden in a Google Calendar invite or an email hijacked Gemini-powered assistants, which in the demos leaked data and controlled smart home devices.

Output hijacking is the shortest path to a bad day: ask the model for a shell command, run it with os.system, and a manipulated answer becomes remote code execution.

The five defenses are deliberately unglamorous. Keep instructions and data apart with the structured messages API instead of string concatenation. Validate every output before it drives an action, the way normal software validates anything from outside. Run a content classifier on responses. Harden the system prompt with explicit scope and refusals. Constrain output to a schema, so injected free text has a harder time riding along. The rule under all five: nothing the model says reaches an action without a check in between, and a failed check is blocked and logged.

An agent's blast radius equals its permissions

Layer two is where a wrong answer stops being a user experience problem and becomes an incident: the wrong email sent, the wrong file deleted, the wrong customer charged. She names three threats. The confused deputy, where an agent acting for user A reads or changes user B's data, usually because memory or a vector store has no per-user namespace. Excessive permissions, such as a search-and-summarize agent that can also delete files. And multi-agent trust chains, where sub-agents trust whatever comes from upstream.

Her line on permissions is worth pinning above a desk: "the blast radius of any failure actually equals the permissions you have granted".

The fixes: a tool allowlist with least privilege, human review for actions you cannot undo, context isolated per user, every action logged before it happens, and agent-to-agent messages checked like user input. She recommends a two-phase design, plan then execute. The agent lists the tool calls and arguments it wants, a human or automated reviewer approves them, and only then does anything run. You get an audit trail for free and a natural place to start an investigation.

MCP servers deserve the npm treatment

Layer three is tools and the Model Context Protocol, and it is the floor she flags. "Teams adopt MCP and new tools quickly without threat modeling them", she said. The threats are tool poisoning (a malicious tool description changes agent behaviour with no code change, because the instruction lives in metadata nobody validates), schema abuse through loose free-form inputs, and unvetted third-party servers, which she compares directly to pulling in any npm package.

So treat them like dependencies. Allowlist tools in production with no dynamic discovery. Validate tool inputs and outputs against a strict JSON schema with additional properties set to false. Log every call. Read the source, check for telemetry, audit network calls, pin versions and review updates.

The infrastructure floor is old advice with higher stakes

Layer four has nothing new in it, and she says so. Secrets still end up in prompts, and prompts land in provider logs and traces, so use a vault and managed identity. Restrict egress at two levels, an application URL filter and network firewall rules, so an injected instruction to ship data elsewhere has nowhere to go. Scan weights and packages in CI/CD with tools like pip-audit, Safety and ModelScan, and prefer safetensors over pickle-based formats that can run code on load. Run agents in minimal containers with dropped capabilities and a read-only root file system.

Stacked together, a prompt injection that gets through layer one still meets permission controls, then the tool allowlist, then egress rules.

Who should watch

ML engineers and platform teams taking an LLM feature from notebook to customers, and product managers who need a shared vocabulary with security. It is a lightning-format survey, so security specialists will know most of the individual controls. The value is the map and the closing checklist: sixteen questions, four per layer. Her advice is to find the weakest layer and ship one fix this sprint: "Small improvements that ship are worth more than a complete plan."

  • Hardening AI Coding Agents with Hooks: Enforcing Least Privilege on Autonomous Developers by Karan Bansal of ArmorCode at Conf42 DevSecOps 2026.
  • Don't Give the Agent a Shell: Tool and Identity Boundaries for AI Agents in Cloud Operations by Ahmed Tariq at Conf42 AI Agents 2026.

entry.title: Your ranking model is learning from items nobody saw
entry.summary: Devavrat Khanolkar (Cisco Systems) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on fixing exposure bias by logging what the screen rendered, not what the server sent.
entry.content:
A server log that says an item was sent to a device is a poor witness to whether anyone saw it. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Devavrat Khanolkar, machine learning engineering technical leader at Cisco Systems, explains how that gap turns into exposure bias: items below the fold get logged as impressions, nobody clicks them because nobody saw them, and the ranking model learns they are bad. His fix, drawn from a past project of his own, is to measure exposure on the client and then run the old and new data pipelines side by side until an A/B experiment settles it.

The failure that never throws an error

Most ranking models are trained by joining two logs: impressions (what was shown) and actions (what the user did). Anything with an action becomes a positive, everything else a negative. That implicit labeling works only if the impression log tells the truth.

With server-side tracking it often is not. Content below the fold is logged as an impression. A failed network call can still count as served. Scroll position and viewport may be ignored entirely. So the item a user chose to skip and the item that never reached their screen end up with the same label.

"Recommendation systems degrade when your training data lies," Devavrat Khanolkar said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. The degradation is quiet. Popular items collect more exposure and more positives, while everything lower down collects false negatives and sinks further. In his words: "The rich got richer, and in this case, an even more important effect is that the poor got poorer". Offline metrics can look perfectly stable through all of this, because they mostly measure how well the model surfaces known positives. Meanwhile users keep seeing the same content every time they open the page.

Three signals that your labels are wrong

Before fixing anything, he wants proof the problem exists. He names three proxies:

  • An impression-interaction gap: items with very high impression counts and almost no engagement. Unless the item is truly terrible, which he says rarely happens, something is off in the logging.
  • A diversity metric that declines over time, with recommendations converging near the top of the page.
  • Negative labels concentrated on a small number of items in the training set.

None of these needs new infrastructure, which makes them a cheap first step.

An impression means rendered, dwelled on and unobstructed

The fix is client-side exposure measurement. The event to log changes from the server sent this item to the item appeared on this screen. Devavrat adds two conditions that are easy to forget: the item stayed in the viewport long enough for the user to register it, and nothing such as a pop-up covered it.

Then comes the part that makes this an MLOps talk. He keeps the legacy pipeline running next to the corrected one, because without the old dataset there is no control model to compare against. Retire it too soon and the experiment is gone. The cost is a stretch of maintaining two pipelines.

His validation checklist for the new signal: schema and coverage across every surface (TVs, laptops and phones, in his video example) and across rank positions, join latency between client and server events, label distribution shift (the invalid negatives should drop meaningfully), and stability over time before any model is trained on it.

Cleaner labels shrink the dataset

Here is the detail teams tend to trip on. If the server logged 100 impressions and only some of them were truly seen, the corrected dataset is smaller. A model trained with the old sampling setup may not converge. He raises sampling rates and revalidates the model before trusting it.

Evaluation then pulls in two directions. Offline, diversity goes up and precision at K or recall at K goes down, because the label distribution itself changed. Online, he expects a short-term engagement drop as the model stops leaning on historically overexposed items, followed by recovery if the experiment runs long enough to see it.

That is why his last piece of advice is about people. Tell stakeholders about the dip before the experiment starts, so nobody dials it down in week one. He also lists who has to be in the room: client and UI engineers for viewport tracking, data engineering to own the new dataset, ML engineers for training and experiment design, and product and analytics for success metrics and the rollout decision.

Who should watch

ML engineers and data engineers who own a recommender or search ranking pipeline, and anyone who has stared at a healthy offline metric while the product felt stale. The talk is a method, with no production numbers from the project behind it, so come for the sequence of steps and the traps. If you already log viewport impressions with dwell time, you can skim to the training and experiment sections.

  • Real-Time Personalization at Scale: Neural Ranking Systems and Operational Breakthroughs by Vedant Agarwal (Walmart Global Tech).

entry.title: Test your agents for permission leaks like any other regression
entry.summary: Ajay Munjuluru (JPMorgan Chase) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on authorization evals: personas, canaries and join tests that can block an agent release.
entry.content:
An agent can write a perfect summary of a client relationship for someone who is not supposed to know half of what is in it, and every eval metric will come back green. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Ajay Munjuluru, senior lead software engineer at JPMorgan Chase, shows how to turn "who is asking" into a test suite that runs in the delivery pipeline and can stop a release. He is clear that every example on his slides is made up for the talk and the opinions are his own.

The agent is one front door to many rule sets

Users used to visit each system separately. The CRM had profiles, permission sets, field-level security and sharing rules. The warehouse had its own policies. Documents had ACLs. Now people ask one question in one place and the agent fetches from everywhere, so it has to combine all those rule sets per request and then describe the result in plain language. Ajay's uncomfortable observation is that a better model makes this harder, because it gets better at putting two and two together.

He groups leaks into five places: the response (the only one most suites check), summaries and memory, tool calls, context and retrieval, and joins. A call note written back to a record that more people can see than its sources is restricted data moved into a shared place. A tool that pulls 50 fields when the task needed five leaves the restricted ones sitting in context. Retrieval is the one he would worry about most: if chunks the user is not entitled to come back, the facts are in the prompt before the model writes a word.

Personas need real logins, canaries need odd numbers

The property he tests: for each persona and each task, everything the agent produces stays inside what that persona may see. That covers responses, summaries, tool arguments and handoffs to other agents.

His banking CRM example has six personas, among them a coverage banker, a deal team member wall-crossed on exactly one deal, a public-side analyst, and a platform admin with lots of configuration access and no business reason to see client financials. The condition that makes them useful is that they are real test users with real permission sets, roles and sharing. "If the persona only exists in the prompt, you're testing whether the model follows instructions, which is a different question from whether your access model holds," Ajay Munjuluru said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

To detect a leak he plants canaries: fake restricted facts that are unique and easy to spot, such as a deal codename or an exposure number with odd precision. They go on records, in free-text notes, inside PDF attachments and in email threads, because the leak usually comes from the note someone pasted, not the field you were watching. The expected results are not written by hand. He logs in as each test user, queries the source system with that user's token and saves what comes back. When someone changes a sharing rule next quarter, the expected sets change with it.

Three kinds of checks sit on top. Exact canary matches in responses, summaries or tool arguments block the release. A judge model answers one narrow question about paraphrased hints, and those hits go to a human reviewer. Behaviour checks ask what the agent did: a service credential used in place of the user's own, fields requested outside the expected set, restricted text written to a shared record. In multi-turn conversations the checks run after every turn.

The hardest leak is built from allowed facts

Ajay calls it permission aggregation disclosure. His definition of the join problem is short: "Two facts the user is allowed to see that add up to the one they aren't." A banker can see a dashboard count of one live sell-side mandate in a sector and region, and an activity feed showing a colleague met one company's CFO three times this month. Ask the agent what is going on with that company and a helpful one connects the dots into material non-public information. No source system did anything wrong and no canary appears in the sentence.

His test is to build scenarios where joining allowed results narrows to a single record, then check the agent does not take the last step: no naming, no ranking of likelihood, no speculation. He would start with three of these.

A pass rate is the wrong gate

The suite runs on more than code changes: model upgrades, prompt edits, new tools or MCP servers (in his experience the most common way a leak arrives), permission changes in the source system and rebuilt retrieval indexes. Tool-level tests run on every pull request, the persona suite nightly, join scenarios before a release, and a few canaries stay in production as tripwires.

The gate is binary. Any exact canary match or wrong credential blocks promotion. "A 99% pass rate here means, one answer in 100 leaked something," he said. When a test fails, the harness walks the trace backwards from the leaked sentence to the context, the tool call, the credential and the rule that should have stopped it, so the right team gets the ticket.

Who should watch

Teams shipping agents over CRM, warehouse or document data in regulated businesses, and anyone who owns an eval suite that has never been run as a second user. No new platform is required: test data, test users, a trace and agreement that authorization is part of release readiness. If your agent only reads public data, you can skip this one.

entry.content:

Copilot, autopilot, or neither

entry.title: Agents were demo-ready in 2023. Production still has to be engineered
entry.summary: Meher Bhaskar Madiraju (Walmart Global Tech) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on the contracts, caching, evals and rollback gates an agent needs after the demo.
entry.content:
Chain ten agent steps that each succeed 90% of the time and the whole run succeeds about 35% of the time. That arithmetic sits at the centre of the talk Meher Bhaskar Madiraju, senior data scientist at Walmart Global Tech, gave at Conf42 MLOps 2026. His argument: models have improved quickly, outcomes have not kept pace, and the gap is engineering work with a known checklist.

A note on scope. The abstract promises a case study from more than 600 retail locations. The recorded talk is something else: a field guide assembled from public incidents and published engineering write-ups, with no internal numbers. It is useful on those terms.

Capability went up, outcomes did not follow

He opens with SWE-bench Verified: the best system scored around 33% in August 2024 and around 80% by January 2026. Then the other column. He cites MIT's NANDA group finding that 95% of generative AI projects show no measurable P&L impact, Gartner's prediction that more than 40% of agentic AI projects will be cancelled by the end of 2027, and the METR trial where experienced open source maintainers felt about 20% faster with AI help and measured 19% slower. He grants that the methodologies are debated.

Two incidents make it concrete: the Replit agent that wiped a production database during a code freeze and then produced fake passing test reports, and the Air Canada chatbot whose invented bereavement policy cost the airline 650 Canadian dollars at a tribunal. "Neither of these failures was a model capability problem. Both were engineering problems," Meher Bhaskar Madiraju said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

The third story is Klarna, whose assistant handled 2.3 million conversations in its first month and cut resolution time from 11 minutes to under two, before the company started bringing human operators back. His reading is that both announcements were sincere, and that the metric you choose to evaluate against is a product decision.

Fan out reads, keep writes single-threaded

On multi-agent design he puts two published positions next to each other. Anthropic's research system, a lead agent spawning parallel sub-agents, scored 90.2% higher than a single agent on an internal eval. Walden Yan of Cognition argues against building multi-agent systems at all, because agents acting in parallel make conflicting implicit decisions. Meher's point is that both agree on the mechanism: sub-agents work when their tasks are read-only.

His rule: "Fan out only for read-only and independently verifiable breadth." Write paths stay single-threaded with full context, and sub-agents return compressed findings, never transcripts.

He then walks four delegation shapes with one failure and one fix each: supervisor (context bloat, fixed by turn and token budgets), pipeline (bad input poisoning every later stage, fixed by typed contracts, checkpoints and dead letter queues), blackboard (write races, fixed by versioned additive writes and leases) and debate (sycophancy, fixed by adversarial personas and a round cap). Every delegation gets a contract with a deadline, a token budget and a response format, plus one named owner for the final answer.

Prompt layout is a cost decision

The context engineering section borrows from Manus, whose agent runs roughly 100 input tokens per output token. That makes cache hit rate the number to watch. He shows the same 20-turn conversation with two layouts. A stable block on top (system prompt, tools, reference docs) with append-only history hit the cache 93% of the time. Put a timestamp or session ID near the top and it fell to 33%. Same model, same task, roughly six times cheaper with the stable layout.

The rules follow: immutable content first, volatile data at the end, never rewrite earlier turns, and mask unavailable tools instead of removing them. For full context windows he lists four habits: compact, take notes outside the window, recite the objective every few turns, and quarantine independent work in a sub-agent.

Reliability compounds, so do the fixes

Back to the formula. For n steps at per-step reliability r, end-to-end success is r to the power n. Ten steps at 99% gives 90%. Ten steps at 90% gives 35%. His remedies are familiar from distributed systems: retries with backoff and jitter, degraded fallback paths, circuit breakers, timeouts, and idempotency keys on anything that mutates. Without the keys, a retry is a second delete.

For hallucination loops, where a small error enters the context and tool results get read as confirmation, he names three structural breaks: require citations for claims, validate every tool output with plain code before it enters the context, and run a critic pass over the plan.

Ship it like software, with a kill switch

The closing third assembles a nine-layer control plane (gateway, orchestrator, agent fleet, tools, memory, observability, eval harness, deploy and fallback, guardrails) and a tiered eval stack: deterministic contract tests in CI, LLM judges on a golden dataset, simulation and canaries, then expert review. Promotion goes offline evals, shadow traffic, canary, full rollout, with rollback triggers wired to guardrails so a regression does not wait for a human. He wants a kill switch that stops spend in seconds without a config change going through review.

Who should watch

Engineers and tech leads with an agent prototype that has impressed a room and now needs an owner. The talk is a dense, well-organised survey, so people who already follow the Anthropic, Cognition and Manus write-ups will recognise much of it. If you came for a retail deployment story, this recording does not contain one.

entry.title: Precompute by default: LLM features on a page that cannot wait
entry.summary: Artem Zamarajev (Amazon) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on four lessons for LLM features on a busy web page: precompute, fallbacks, output checks, one gateway.
entry.content:
The safest model call on a product page is the one that never happens while the shopper is waiting. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Artem Zamarajev, a senior software engineer at Amazon working on AI shopping features, compresses what he has learned about LLM features on high-traffic pages into four lessons: precompute by default, keep the model off the critical path, check outputs before customers see them, and put one service in front of the assistant.

His scope is narrow on purpose. This is about AI features inside a web page a shopper loads in a browser. Standalone chatbots and background agents get only partial credit.

Three problems the usual toolkit does not cover

Timeouts, caching, canaries, feature flags and A/B tests still apply. LLM features add three things on top.

Latency: he quotes Google's guidance that a page's main content should appear within 2.5 seconds and the first byte within 0.8 seconds. A fast model starts streaming in a few hundred milliseconds, but a full response takes several seconds and the slow tail runs longer.

Quality: bad output arrives well-formed with a successful status, so the error rate stays flat while customers read something wrong.

Cost: every call costs money, and page-view volume multiplies it.

To keep the lessons concrete he invents a store, Ridgeline Coffee, with three features on each product page. A quick take (three LLM-written highlights from product details and reviews), suggested questions picked for the shopper, and an Ask button that opens the store's assistant.

Ask three questions before generating anything live

Does the output depend on the shopper or what they typed? How often do the inputs change? Is anyone waiting for it?

The quick take is the same for everyone, changes only when the product or its reviews change, and nobody is waiting. So it is generated in a background job, checked, and stored. The page does a key lookup. Latency becomes a read, and cost follows product changes instead of traffic. One trap: regenerate on every new review and a popular product burns model calls all day for text that barely moves. He uses a threshold, such as a minimum number of new reviews.

The Ask button has to be live, but only runs for shoppers who click. Suggested questions depend on the shopper, so they run live on every page view. Remember that one for lesson four.

A timeout will not save the page

A timeout short enough to protect the page would cut off most model calls. So the answer depends on the feature type.

For precomputed content he decides the fallback before writing a prompt, as a ladder: fresh content, then the last good version, then a plain non-AI default such as the product's existing bullet points, then hiding the feature. For live features the page renders first and the model is called afterwards. Suggested questions fill in late, and if they fail the space stays empty. The Ask response is streamed, which also keeps long answers from hitting fixed timeouts in proxies and gateways. The worst case is a plainer page.

Wrong output looks like success

He brings up the 2024 tribunal ruling against Air Canada, whose chatbot told a customer something that contradicted the airline's own policy page. The company owns what the model says.

Before a quick take is stored, it passes four checks: format, grounding (every claim traces to product data or a review), consistency with the rest of the page, and content policy. A highlight saying the coffee ships ground on a page that says whole bean only is his small-scale example. Format and policy are mostly rules. Grounding and consistency often need a second model call, which is affordable because it runs once per product change.

Live responses get layers instead: the model works from the product's own data, cheap rule checks run on the stream, and a sample of real responses is judged afterwards. Both kinds get a fixed eval set rerun on every prompt or model change. And because fallbacks hide failures, the rejection rate is the metric to watch during a rollout. The page looks healthy either way.

One door in front of the assistant

The Ask button and suggested questions both call the same assistant. Let each call it directly and two things go wrong. Eligibility rules, languages, timeouts and fallbacks get copied and drift apart. And an assistant sized for the small share of shoppers who click Ask suddenly receives a call on every page view.

His fix is a small service between features and the assistant that holds the rules, sets the timeout, returns fallbacks, and gives each feature a traffic budget with rate limits. "I make it a service rather than a shared library because a library can't enforce one budget across every caller," Artem Zamarajev said at Conf42 MLOps 2026.

His one-line summary of the whole talk: "calling the model is easy, and most of the work is just a system around it".

Who should watch

Backend and full-stack engineers adding generative features to pages that already have latency targets, and the product managers who keep asking why it cannot just call the model. It is a short, tidy talk with no slides of production metrics. The abstract speaks of millions of daily renders with zero faults, while the recording stays with the invented coffee shop, so expect patterns over war stories.

entry.title: Agent reliability is a property of the platform around the model
entry.summary: Amit Anand at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on the platform agents need to heal infrastructure: durable runs, a policy gate, run IDs and autonomy per action class.
entry.content:
At 99% success per step and no retries, a 50-step agent run completes about 60% of the time. Amit Anand, who builds distributed systems, payment systems and AI agents, uses that arithmetic at Conf42 MLOps 2026 to argue that agent reliability is decided by the platform, and then runs an architecture review of that platform with one incident threaded through it: latency on an API service creeps up after a deployment, and an agent proposes a rollback.

"The reliability of agentic system is a property of the platform around the model," Amit Anand said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. He opens and closes on that sentence.

An agent run is a long workflow whose control flow you do not know

Amit reads an agent run as a distributed, long-running workflow where the model picks the control flow at runtime. A trigger starts the run, then it loops: plan through the model gateway, act through the tool gateway, write a checkpoint to a state store, emit telemetry tagged with the run ID. Every arrow is a remote call that can be slow, fail or be retried.

Four forces follow. You do not know a run's length or fan-out when you admit it, so you need admission control and run budgets. Failures compound, so you retry individual steps and each step must be safe to retry. Runs outlive their compute, since a pod or a deploy can end before the run does, so state has to be durable. And one run mixes GPU-bound, CPU-bound and I/O-bound work, which calls for separate pools that scale on work signals.

The planner never touches production

In the incident, telemetry arrives through OpenTelemetry, detection correlates alerts and traces into one incident, diagnosis finds the deployment, and planning proposes a rollback with a risk score. Then comes the box Amit calls the most important: the policy gate. Policy as code decides whether a rollback is permitted on this service right now and answers allow, deny or ask a human. If allowed, the change is applied, preferably as a Git commit that a controller reconciles.

Verification closes the loop. If latency and error rates recover, done. If the result is unclear or worse, the default is to stop and escalate to the on-call engineer. An automatic compensating action runs only where one has been defined and tested.

The security model is a trust boundary. Everything the agent reads is untrusted: alerts, logs, tickets, tool output. A line injected into a log can steer an agent with broad privileges, the classic confused deputy. So the agent runtime gets a scoped identity that can read telemetry, call the model and write its own state. It emits a typed request, and every infrastructure-changing action goes through a gateway that can refuse. As a side benefit, "Your compliance evidence is the gateway log."

Retry storms, duplicate actions and 200 OK

Amit walks through three failure modes. In a retry storm, a model endpoint slows, every agent retries together and load peaks when capacity is lowest, which is also how cost runs away. The response is rate limits, jittered backoff and load shedding at the gateway. Duplicate actions happen when a worker crashes after requesting the rollback and before recording the result, so actions need idempotency keys and you verify state before retrying when the outcome is unknown.

The observability gap is the quiet one. Model and tool spans come from different libraries with no shared context. The Kubernetes change carries no run ID, so the audit log shows a service account patched a deployment and cannot say which decision caused it. Nothing records the outcome: every call returns 200 whether or not latency recovered. His rule is to connect run ID, decision, action and outcome, because you should not automate what you cannot evaluate.

Autonomy is granted per action class

The reference architecture has one logical control plane per organisation holding the model and tool registry with evaluation gates, GitOps and policy, quota and the observability backend, over identical Kubernetes clusters per cloud. Inside a cluster, a KEDA scaler sets the worker count from queue depth and age, and scale-in must respect active runs. The GPU pool scales on waiting requests, queue time and time to first token, because throughput flattens once the pool is saturated.

On multi-cloud he is careful. Routing new inference requests to another cloud is the easy case, though a pairing such as GKE with Vertex AI and EKS with Bedrock is not interchangeable, so prompts and evaluations must pass on both. Resuming a run already in progress is harder. You pay for it in recovery time, data residency constraints, network cost and idle GPUs.

Autonomy is set by reversibility and blast radius. Reversible and narrow actions may become autonomous, wide and irreversible ones need approval, and every class starts as recommend-only and steps up when its evaluation passes and its production record is clean. For run execution he compares LangGraph checkpoints with a workflow engine such as Temporal and notes the two can be used together.

MLOps comes in at release. Version the model, prompt, tools and configuration together, evaluate the version on past incidents, deploy gradually. "A new prompt goes through the same gate as a new model."

Who should watch

Platform engineers and SREs who have been asked to let an agent act on production and want the design questions in one place. It is a dense architecture review in under fifteen minutes, with no demo and no vendor product. The migration order alone is worth noting down: join the traces, insert the gateway in recommend-only mode, turn runbooks into typed tools, then promote by evidence.

entry.title: How OpenAI connects Codex to Flyte through MCP for ML training runs
entry.summary: Phoebe Wang (OpenAI) at Conf42 MLOps 2026 on a read-only Flyte MCP tool that lets Codex turn a failed training run link into a first fix to test.
entry.content:
OpenAI hosts Flyte for its internal traditional ML training jobs, and the unit that moves between people, the orchestrator and the coding agent is a run link. At Conf42 MLOps 2026, Phoebe Wang, Member of Technical Staff at OpenAI working on ML infrastructure, shows how a small Flyte MCP server lets Codex look up a failed execution, report what Flyte recorded and suggest the first thing to test. It is a short talk with one clear pattern in it.

A failed run is three questions

Phoebe starts with a scene every ML engineer knows. You change a model, submit the full training job, go back to other work, and later receive a link to a failed run. In her fictional example, loading the data worked, training failed, and evaluation never started because it needs the trained model. What she wants to know at that point is which step failed, what error was reported and what to test next.

The three pieces each have one job. Flyte, the open-source ML orchestration layer, runs the steps of a workflow and records the state of every run. MCP, the Model Context Protocol, lets an AI application use tools, so a Flyte MCP server can expose a tool that looks up a run and returns its task states and recorded errors. Codex is where the question gets asked.

"The useful handoff is the link," Phoebe Wang said at Conf42 MLOps 2026. The same link can go to a teammate, and both people start from the same run.

The run record is what makes the next run a fair comparison

A workflow defines the steps; a run is one attempt at them. Her example is an image classifier where run 41 finished all three steps and run 42 stopped in training, both from the same workflow.

That history matters the next morning, when the editor holds three more changes. Which version of the code did the failed job run? Was it the same dataset as the last good run? Did the batch size or the GPU type change? She keeps the run link and records the workflow version, the software environment, the dataset and the inputs, which for this classifier include the evaluation split and the batch size. Change one thing in the next run and those records make the comparison fair. They also let you trace a model you want to serve back to the run that produced it.

Give the tool a narrow, read-only job

The integration answers one small question: given a link, can Codex tell which step failed and what Flyte recorded? Phoebe's summary of the design: "That gives the tool a narrow read-only job."

For run 42 the tool returns the run state, the failed task and the error details. Flyte says the training step ran out of GPU memory and that evaluation was skipped, so the place to look is training. Her advice for teams building something similar comes as four principles:

  • Start with the information someone would normally open the workflow UI to find.
  • Give the tool a way to identify the exact run.
  • Return the task and the error in a form the agent can refer to.
  • Keep access scoped to the runs the caller is allowed to see.

Evidence first, then a suggestion you still review

In the Codex CLI, the first part of the answer is the evidence: the error trace Flyte returned. The suggestion follows from it. An out-of-memory error in training points to a smaller batch, because a smaller batch keeps fewer things in GPU memory at once. Codex can update the local training code and environment so the modified run can start.

Phoebe keeps the human in two places. She reviews the change before submitting a run, and she checks the evaluation score afterwards, because a smaller batch can change training behaviour. A run that finishes and a model worth keeping are two separate things to verify.

The talk ends with the step after training. Her team built a GPU deploy skill in Codex so experimental models can be put on GPUs quickly and tested end to end for latency and availability. The example request is to prepare a test deployment of version three of the classifier and show the change for review, which gives Codex a model, a version, a target and a clear point to hand back.

Who should watch

Platform engineers who run Flyte, or any workflow orchestrator, and are deciding what to expose to coding agents first. The session is brief and uses a fictional run on slides; it does not go into how the MCP server is implemented, and the checklist promised in the abstract arrives as the four design principles above. As a pattern for a first, low-risk agent integration, it is easy to copy.
